summary: Pupils aged 9–10 learn to separate mixtures by reasoning from a PROPERTY DIFFERENCE to a technique: particle size → sieve; insolubility → filter; solubility → evaporate; magnetism → magnet. The central skill is planning an ORDERED sequence for multi-component mixtures (e.g. sand + salt + water: filter out insoluble sand, then evaporate the filtrate to recover dissolved salt) and justifying each step by the property it exploits — not reciting a recipe. A persistent confusion to address directly is filtering (removes insoluble solids) versus evaporating (recovers dissolved solids).
misconceptions: Filtering can separate a dissolved solid from its solution (it passes straight through).
Sieving and filtering are the same technique.
Evaporating destroys the dissolved solid rather than leaving it behind.
Any mixture can be separated by a single step, ignoring the need for a sequence.
The order of steps does not matter.

activities.title: Plan an ordered separation for sand + salt + water
steps: Start with one beaker holding sand + salt + water and the goal: recover a clean, dry pile of sand AND a clean, dry pile of salt, separated from each other.
Before acting, tag each component with its relevant property: sand = insoluble solid, salt = dissolved (soluble) solid, water = liquid.
Choose an order of techniques from available stations/apparatus (sieve, filter funnel, evaporating dish, magnet) and carry it out.
Filter first: observe that the insoluble sand stays on the filter paper while the salty water passes through; rinse and dry the sand.

Then evaporate the filtered salt-water: observe the water level falling as the water leaves as invisible water vapour (any visible 'steam' is tiny droplets formed as the vapour cools), and salt crystals remaining behind once the water has gone.

Deliberately try the wrong order (evaporate before filtering) and observe the result: the water leaves and you are back to a dry sand-and-salt mixture with the salt crystallised among the grains — there is no simple DRY way to separate them, so you would have to add water again and start over.
State, for each step, which property difference it exploits.
activities.insight: The order matters because each method depends on a specific property difference: the insoluble sand must be filtered out first. If the water is evaporated too early, the dissolved salt crystallises among the sand grains, leaving a dry mixture with no simple way to separate the two solids — you would have to re-dissolve and start over, wasting the step. Method choice follows from properties, not memory.

activities.title: Transfer: choose a method for a new mixture by its property
steps: Face a different mixture, e.g. iron filings mixed with sand, and decide how to separate it.
Name the property difference being exploited (here, magnetism: iron is magnetic, sand is not) and choose the matching method (a magnet).
Try other new mixtures (e.g. gravel + sand needing a sieve for particle size; a dissolved solid needing evaporation) and justify each method by the property difference.
Explain why a method would fail if the property it relies on were absent (e.g. a magnet does nothing for two non-magnetic solids).
activities.insight: A separation method is chosen because of a specific property difference between components; the same reasoning transfers to any mixture, so the learner is not bound to one memorised sequence.

activities.title: Apparatus reference: what each tool separates and why
steps: Study each piece of apparatus — sieve, filter funnel, evaporating dish, magnet — and state what it separates (large bits from small; insoluble solid from liquid; dissolved solid from solution; magnetic from non-magnetic).
For each, name the property that makes it work and sketch or label where each component ends up.
Link each tool back to the mixtures it would suit.
activities.insight: Each separation tool exploits one property difference, and knowing which property each relies on is what makes it possible to plan a correct sequence.

activities.title: Explain and defend the plan (discussion probes)
steps: After separating, answer: 'Why did you filter before evaporating and not the other way round? What would go wrong if you swapped them?'
Answer: 'The water that came through the filter — is it pure, or is something still in it? How do you know?'
Answer: 'If it were iron filings mixed with sand instead, what would you use, and why?'
Answer: 'Which property of each substance is each of your steps taking advantage of?'
activities.insight: Justifying the sequence aloud reveals whether the learner understands the property basis of each step or is reproducing a remembered recipe.

checkQuestion: Hand the child a beaker holding a mixture of sand and salt in water, with filter paper + funnel, an empty beaker, and an evaporating dish over gentle heat available. Say: 'Get me back a clean pile of dry sand AND a clean pile of dry salt, both separated from each other. Show me your steps.' Watch the ORDER they choose and what they do at each stage — do not tell them the sequence.
checkAnswer: Filter FIRST: the sand stays on the filter paper (insoluble), the salt-water solution passes through into the beaker. Rinse/dry the sand. Then EVAPORATE the filtered solution so the water leaves and dry salt is recovered. The critical move is filtering before evaporating — the child must exploit that sand is insoluble and salt is dissolved.
